description: Team USV builds Earshot, which turns NASA's Earth maps into sound so that people who are blind or have low vision can hear where the smoke, haze, rain and warm seas are, and what has changed. We care about accessibility, Earth science and clear design. Our skills: web development, audio, data visualization and science communication. Teammates who know screen readers, sound design or teaching are welcome.
summary: Earshot turns NASA's Earth maps into music that people who are blind or have low vision can read by ear. About 28,000 people in Charlotte, and 8.6 million across the United States, are blind or have serious difficulty seeing, yet NASA's Earth Information Center tells the story of our planet in pictures. Earshot is the jukebox the challenge asks for: it pairs Earth Information Center frames (night lights from 2012 to 2023, ocean currents, aerosols, lightning, fine particles) and the newest day of rain, smoke, haze and sea temperature from NASA GIBS with sound computed from the data the moment you press play. Low notes are the south, high notes the north; the sound moves from your left ear to your right, west to east; louder and brighter means more. One button plays only what changed over twelve years. Type your city to hear the area around it, with a chime where you are, and a sentence saying how far away and in which direction the most smoke or haze is. Earshot reads the real number behind each colour from NASA's own colour tables, speaks a plain briefing, works with a screen reader and keyboard, and can turn its own sound back into the map. Its design follows published studies of sound maps with blind listeners.
details:
The problem

NASA's Earth Information Center shows our changing planet in beautiful pictures. If you cannot see the picture, you get a caption or nothing. About 28,000 people in Charlotte and 8.6 million across the United States are blind or have serious difficulty seeing, even with glasses (US Census Bureau, American Community Survey 2024). Worldwide, 43 million people are blind and 295 million more have moderate or severe vision loss (The Lancet Global Health, 2021). For them a smoke map is a closed door, even on the day the smoke is over their own city.

What Earshot is

Earshot is an Earth Information Jukebox. It pairs NASA Earth Information Center frames with sound made from the data, in real time, in the browser. The picture stays on screen for people who can see it, and the sound carries the same information for everyone else.

How to listen: three rules

  1. Low notes are the south of the planet, high notes the north.
  2. The sound travels from your left ear to your right, from west to east.
  3. Louder and brighter means more. A soft hiss means there is no data there.

What you can do

  • Play the jukebox: night lights from 2012 to 2023, ocean currents and temperature, four kinds of aerosol (dust, smoke, sulfate, sea salt), lightning seen from the International Space Station, and fine particles (PM2.5). Plus the newest day of rain, smoke and dust, haze and sea temperature, read live from NASA GIBS.
  • Hear the planet change: play all 12 years of night lights in order, then press "Hear only what changed". Only the places where light grew make a sound, and Earshot says in one sentence where the largest rise was.
  • Ask about your own place: type a city to hear its value in words. Then hear the area around it, with a soft chime as the sound passes you. Earshot says how far away and in which direction the most smoke, haze or rain is.
  • Make it easy: hear one band of the planet at a time, four voices together, or all eight. Pick another instrument if you prefer.
  • Read it in words: a plain briefing of each map, a description of each picture, an optional page voice, and vibration on phones.
  • Test your ear: a one-minute listening check, eyes closed, shows whether you can hear the map.
  • Take it with you: download any map as a sound file. The file carries a small note, so dropping it back into Earshot turns the sound back into the map.
  • Bring your own data: a world map picture or a table of places and values. It stays in your browser.
  • Every day, anywhere: a daily audio feed for any city, an open web API with free keys for other apps, and an MCP server that lets AI assistants read NASA's maps.
  • In class: a twenty-minute teachers' guide for students who are blind, have low vision or see well, together.

How it works

Earshot does not guess from colours. For the day-by-day maps it turns each colour back into its real number using NASA's own GIBS colour tables, so a reading of 2.3 means an aerosol optical depth of 2.3, not "orange". Each map is measured in 8 bands from south to north and 72 slices from west to east. Each band is a voice in one calm chord, and the sound sweeps across the slices in about twelve seconds. Each kind of map has its own instrument so you can tell records apart; rain patters and lightning crackles faster where there is more. After making each sound, Earshot hands only the audio to a second program, which rebuilds the map from what it hears. On every record the rebuilt map matches the original almost exactly (0.998 or better), so the sound really carries the data.

Built on research with blind listeners

  • Sweep, speech and keyboard together: with a sound map that combined all three, seven blind users completed 95% of geography tasks, against 33% with a spreadsheet (Zhao, Plaisant, Shneiderman and Lazar, 2008). Earshot gives the same three ways in.
  • Sound maps work for blind people: 35 people, 20 of them blind, explored sound maps and then picked the matching tactile map with high accuracy, with no difference between blind and sighted listeners (Delogu and others, 2010).
  • Fewer voices at once: following three or more steady sounds is very hard, and patterned sounds help keep them apart (Flowers, 2005). Earshot starts with four voices, each with its own shimmer, and offers one band at a time.
  • Loudness alone carries numbers poorly (Neuhoff, 2011), so a bigger value is both louder and brighter.
  • Left and right are easy to miss: only one of seven blind users consciously used them (Zhao and others, 2008). So the sweep always starts in the west, and Earshot also says the direction in words.
  • NASA's own sonifications reach this audience: in a survey of 3,184 people, sighted, blind and low-vision people reported learning from them (Arcand and others, 2024).

What is new

NASA's sonifications and earlier projects, including Arcobaleno, a 2023 Space Apps global winner, turned pictures into sound. Earshot adds five things: the real value behind each colour, from NASA's colour tables; a check that turns every sound back into its map; the area around your own place every day, with distance and direction; sound files that become maps again; and hearing only what changed.

Who it helps, and how they would get it

Through tools they already use: the website, with a screen reader, a keyboard or a phone; a daily audio feed for their own city; a classroom, with the teachers' guide; a speaker beside the Earth Information Center wall playing the whole jukebox; and other apps, through the open API. It is free, open source (Apache 2.0), runs in any modern browser, and needs no install and no account. In Charlotte it matters most for air quality: on a smoky day, a blind resident can hear where the smoke is and which way it lies from home.

What is next

Tune the sounds with blind and low-vision listeners and teachers in Charlotte, add more Earth Information Center records, and speak the briefings in more languages.

Tools

HTML, CSS and JavaScript with no frameworks; the Web Audio, Web Speech and Vibration APIs; Node.js with no packages; hosted on Amazon Web Services (EC2 behind CloudFront). Source code: https://github.com/usv240/earshot-space-apps . Demo video: https://dp16xommhs4bv.cloudfront.net/demo.html . Seven slides: https://dp16xommhs4bv.cloudfront.net/slides.html . Teachers' guide: https://dp16xommhs4bv.cloudfront.net/teachers.html

Use of AI

An AI assistant (Claude, by Anthropic, through Claude Code) was used heavily: it researched the challenge, the rules and earlier work, proposed technical approaches, and wrote most of the code, the site text, the slides and the video script. The team chose the challenge, the audience (people who are blind or have low vision), the focus on daily information about the place where you live, bringing your own data, an open API, grounding the design in published research, and the hosting, and decided what stayed. No image, video or sound was made by generative AI: every sound is computed from NASA data by Earshot's own code, the demo narration is a standard computer voice, and every source file is marked as written with AI assistance.
